claims.text: Protective oxide development and retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by formation of a stable, slow-growing oxide layer.
The multi-component composition of high-entropy alloys enhances segregation of oxide-forming elements to the surface.
Enhanced surface segregation of oxide-forming elements promotes growth of a dense oxide layer.
Enhanced surface segregation of oxide-forming elements promotes growth of an adherent oxide layer.
Surface segregation of oxide-forming elements leads to formation of a stable, slow-growing oxide layer.
Oxide-layer thickness and composition are the structural mediators of oxidation behavior.
After exposure at 1000°C in air for 100 hours, the high-entropy alloy will have an oxide layer 30% thinner than that of traditional alloys.
After exposure at 1000°C in air for 100 hours, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit 25% greater oxidation resistance than traditional alloys.
Oxidation resistance can be assessed from oxidation-induced weight gain.
Traditional alloys, including Ni-based superalloys, exposed under identical conditions provide the baseline comparison.
The proposed behavior applies in air at temperatures above 800°C.
The exact high-entropy-alloy composition may influence protective-oxide formation and stability.
Processing history may influence protective-oxide formation and stability.
An oxide thickness greater than 10 μm after 100 hours would falsify the hypothesis.
An oxidation weight gain greater than 5 mg/cm² after 100 hours would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction is defined relative to traditional-alloy performance, whereas falsification uses absolute thresholds of 10 μm and 5 mg/cm² without reference to the baseline. Consequently, the stated relative prediction could fail without crossing either threshold, or an alloy could outperform the baseline yet be declared falsified.

A 25% increase in oxidation resistance is said to be measured by weight gain, but no resistance metric or required direction and magnitude of weight-gain change is defined. Weight gain itself is normally an oxidation measure for which lower, not higher, values imply improved resistance.
